newsitem.title: USA: Fed faces challenge in easing inflation doubts.
newsitem.headline: Fed faces challenge in easing inflation doubts.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan last week expressed optimism about the inflation picture in major nations, but U.S. investors question whether steady prices are here to stay.

Speaking on Friday at a symposium entitled "Achieving Price Stability," Greenspan credited central bankers with making huge strides in bringing down inflation from its "corrosive" double-digit levels in the early 1980s.

"Now, for the first time in at least a generation, the goal of price stability is within reach of all the major industrial countries as well as a substantial number of others," the Fed chief proclaimed.

The symposium, an annual event sponsored by the Kansas City Fed that typically garners a great deal of attention in financial markets, was attended by central bankers and economists from around the world.

Greenspan was among several participants in the symposium to remark on the progress made in containing prices. Inflation in many European countries is hovering near 3 percent and has been even lower in Japan.
In the United States, inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index has remained below 3 percent for four years straight -- the best performance since the 1960s.

The long-term picture, however, offered little comfort to U.S. investors as they fretted last week about the latest economic data showing a surge in new home sales and signs of strength in the manufacturing sector.

Stock and bond traders are worried that the lively economic activity could lead to a pickup in inflation, which erodes returns on investments. Many are also bracing for a possible interest-rate rise by the Fed to head off such pressures.

The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond closed down nearly a point on Friday as its yield, which moves in the opposite direction of the price, closed the week at 7.12 percent -- above the key psychological level of 7 percent.
The Dow Jones industrial average fell more than 106 points last week, to finish Friday at 5,616.

Although signs of robust growth began emerging in the early months of this year, the Fed's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee has opted to hold rates steady on the expectation that the situation was temporary and would not cause a pickup in prices.
Some experts have begun to question whether that stance is appropriate.

Martin Feldstein of Harvard University, a prominent economist who heads the National Bureau of Economic Research, voiced such concerns in the presence of Greenspan and several of his colleagues on the FOMC who were at the symposium.
"I think there is a strong case for increasing interest rates in order to prevent an increase in inflation," Felstein said.
But he added that he believed the Fed would be hamstrung by political considerations and a lack of support outside the investment community for higher rates.
For their part, the Fed officials present did not comment on the remark. Nor did they give any indication publicly of where they were leaning on interest rates.
But the situation highlights the difficulty the Fed faces, despite the stellar inflation performance recently, in convincing the markets that it is committed to keeping prices in check.

"It has been an excellent inflation performance in the past 15 years but there are these nagging doubts in the financial markets," said Lawrence Kudlow, economic counsel for A.B. Laffer, V.A. Canto and Associates.
"If ordinary people were convinced the United States had embarked on a path of price stability, long-term rates would be lower," he added.
Former Fed Vice Chairman David Mullins described the current situation as a pivotal period for the U.S. central bank concerning expectations about inflation.

"We're on the cusp of a regime shift," said Mullins, who is now a principal at Long-Term Capital Management LP. "The market is uncertain whether we're going to retrace the inflation rates of the 1970s."
